scope: Eight source-grounded historical scientists; identities checked against linked catalogue works. No dist files modified by this research pass.

entries.name: René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur
entries.short: French naturalist and experimental scientist who studied insects, metallurgy and the measurement of temperature.
entries.biography: René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur was a French naturalist and experimental scientist whose interests linked living organisms, materials and useful manufacturing techniques. Born in La Rochelle, he moved to Paris in 1703 and entered the Académie royale des sciences in 1708 after studying mathematics. From 1711 he worked on the Academy’s descriptions of arts and trades, investigating iron and steel production and later porcelain. In 1730 he proposed rules for making comparable thermometers, and his alcohol thermometer gave its name to a temperature scale. His six-volume Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire des insectes, published from 1734 to 1742, made detailed observation of insect life a major scientific undertaking. The catalogue’s Insecte des limaçons belongs to this broader programme of natural-history research; “Reaumub” is an OCR variant of his surname.

entries.name: Pierre-Louis Dulong
entries.short: French physicist and chemist known for precise measurements of heat, gases and the Dulong–Petit relation.
entries.biography: Pierre-Louis Dulong was a French physicist and chemist trained initially in medicine. He entered the École polytechnique as a teenager and subsequently worked in Claude-Louis Berthollet’s laboratory and with Louis-Jacques Thénard. His research ranged from chemical reactions to the behaviour of heat and gases. With Alexis-Thérèse Petit he investigated cooling, temperature measurement and the heat capacities of substances; their collaboration is remembered in the Dulong–Petit relation. He also worked with Jöns Jacob Berzelius on the composition of water and with François Arago on steam pressure. Dulong taught physics at Polytechnique from 1820 to 1829 and directed its studies from 1830 until his death. The catalogue’s papers on heat, gaseous fluids and work with Petit and Thénard strongly identify this Dulong despite the stray initial “J”.

The 1843 Recherches sur la chaleur is a posthumous publication; the “J” initial is not a reason to create another scientist. One Cabart-authored record only mentions Dulong and is flagged separately.

entries.name: Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau
entries.short: French chemist, teacher and politician who helped reform chemical nomenclature and establish the École polytechnique.
entries.biography: Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau combined chemistry, teaching and public life. Originally a lawyer in Dijon, he established a laboratory, gave public chemistry courses and corresponded with researchers across Europe. With Hugues Maret and Jean-François Durande he produced the Élémens de chymie théorique et pratique, published at Dijon in 1777–1778 to support those courses. His concern with clear chemical terminology helped prepare the later reform of chemical nomenclature. After discussions with Lavoisier he adopted the new chemistry that displaced phlogiston explanations. During the French Revolution he served in the Legislative Assembly and National Convention and participated in scientific work for national defence. He helped establish the institution that became the École polytechnique, taught chemistry there and served as its director from 1799 to 1804. His practical interests also included disinfecting air.

entries.name: Heinrich Rose
entries.short: German analytical chemist whose mineral studies and teaching manuals helped establish systematic chemical analysis.
entries.biography: Heinrich Rose was a German chemist and pharmacist associated with the University of Berlin. He came from a family of pharmacists and chemists and learned analytical methods from Martin Heinrich Klaproth before continuing his training with Jöns Jacob Berzelius in Stockholm. Research on titanium compounds and minerals led to his doctorate at Kiel in 1821. He began teaching in Berlin in 1822 and became a full professor of chemistry in 1835. His work concentrated on identifying and separating the constituents of inorganic substances, and his textbooks became important guides to analytical practice. French translations published his name as Henri Rose, the form used on many of the catalogue cards. He should be distinguished from his younger brother Gustav Rose, a mineralogist with a separate scientific career.

entries.name: Friedrich Wöhler
entries.short: German chemist known for preparing urea in the laboratory and for influential work in organic and inorganic chemistry.
entries.biography: Friedrich Wöhler was a German chemist whose career joined laboratory teaching with wide-ranging experimental research. After medical training he worked with Jöns Jacob Berzelius in Stockholm, then developed a long collaboration with Justus von Liebig. In 1828 he obtained urea while studying cyanate chemistry, a celebrated demonstration that a substance associated with living organisms could be prepared in the laboratory. His work was broader than that episode: he investigated minerals and elements as well as organic compounds, and with Liebig studied uric acid and bitter-almond oil. Appointed professor of pharmacy and chemistry at Göttingen in 1836, he helped make its teaching laboratory internationally influential. The collection includes the French version of his 1828 urea paper, investigations of titanium and aluminium, and an inorganic-analysis handbook; “Friedricb Wôhler” is a transcription variant.

entries.name: Henri Pellat
entries.short: French physicist and Sorbonne teacher whose work addressed electrical potential, dielectrics and physical measurement.
entries.biography: Henri Pellat was a French physicist who taught at the Sorbonne and worked on experimental questions in electricity and physical measurement. His publications examine the potential difference between metals in contact, the behaviour of insulating materials in electric fields, electrolysis and electrical discharges in rarefied gases. He also wrote and taught beyond electricity: the École normale supérieure preserves manuscript notes of his thermodynamics course from 1896–1897. His public role included directing the Ministry of Commerce and Industry’s office for checking alcohol-measuring instruments, and he reported on precision instruments at the Paris exhibition of 1900. The catalogue reflects both laboratory research and teaching through papers, a doctoral thesis, and lecture volumes on electricity, polarisation and thermodynamics. The forms “Henrl Pellat” and “Henr i Pellat” represent transcription variants of Henri.

entries.name: Władysław Natanson
entries.short: Polish theoretical physicist at the Jagiellonian University who studied thermodynamics, viscous fluids, radiation and optics.
entries.biography: Władysław Natanson was a Polish theoretical physicist whose publications also used the name Ladislaus Natanson. After studies in Saint Petersburg and Dorpat and periods with J. J. Thomson in Cambridge and Ludwig Boltzmann in Graz, he settled in Kraków. He qualified to teach at the Jagiellonian University in 1891 and became professor of theoretical physics in 1902. His early work concerned the kinetic theory of gases; he subsequently investigated irreversible processes and their application to the motion of viscous fluids. Later interests included electron theory, radiation and the passage of light through gases. A 1911 study examined the statistical treatment of indistinguishable radiation quanta. The catalogue’s German papers on dissipation, viscosity, thermodynamic potentials and irreversible processes correspond closely to this programme. The Polish form “Wład. Natansona” is an inflected abbreviated name.

entries.name: Carlo Matteucci
entries.short: Italian physicist and physiologist whose experiments helped establish the study of electrical activity in living tissue.
entries.biography: Carlo Matteucci was an Italian physicist and physiologist, often called Charles Matteucci in French publications. His experiments investigated electrical currents in animal tissues and the relationship between muscle activity and electricity, making him an important early figure in electrophysiology. Appointed to the chair of experimental physics at Pisa in 1840, he developed a laboratory intended for research as well as teaching and acquired instruments in Paris for the university. His interests also extended to electromagnetic induction, magnetism, meteorology and telegraphy. He helped found Il Cimento in 1844; the journal was later revived as Il Nuovo Cimento. Matteucci also served as Italy’s minister of public instruction in 1862. The collection’s French and Italian works on animal electricity, nerve currents, induction and physics lectures belong to this scientist, not the later namesake previously attached to “Charles”.
